summary: This standards-track RFC sets out the requirements and considerations for WebRTC applications that send and receive video. It specifies the video processing needed and which video codecs and parameters must be supported so browsers and other WebRTC endpoints can interoperate.

eli5.summary: When two apps make a video call, they must agree on a language for pictures. This lists the languages every app must understand so calls always work.

questions: which video codecs must webrtc support
what video codecs must webrtc support
subtitle: Which video codecs every WebRTC browser must support, and the processing rules that make video calls interoperate.

tldr.problem: Two WebRTC endpoints can only show each other video if they agree on how it is captured, oriented, encoded and decoded. Without a common baseline, calls between different implementations could fail.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC makes VP8 and H.264 Constrained Baseline mandatory to implement for WebRTC browsers, sets defaults such as the sRGB color space and Y'CbCr 4:2:0 scan, requires receivers to handle changing resolution and orientation, and fixes the H.264 parameter settings.
tldr.outcome: Any WebRTC browser can be expected to speak at least VP8 and H.264, with the same defaults. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 7742 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the published definition of the WebRTC video requirements.

sections.title: Scope of the Video Rules
sections.content:
Sending and receiving interactive video is one of the major functions of WebRTC endpoints. The video might come from a camera, a screen recording, a stored file or some other source. RFC 7742 gives the requirements and considerations for WebRTC applications that send and receive it, including the video processing that is required and the video codecs and their parameters.

It covers only video-codec handling. How media streams are carried across the network is left to a separate document on WebRTC media transport and the use of RTP.
sections.eli5: This is the rulebook for the picture part of a video call: how the picture is made, tilted and packed up. How it travels is somebody else's rulebook.

sections.title: Kinds of WebRTC Endpoints
sections.content:
The RFC uses the key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in RFC 2119. It also defines four kinds of endpoint, because the codec rules differ between them.

  • A WebRTC browser (or WebRTC user agent) conforms to both the protocol specification and the JavaScript API.
  • A WebRTC non-browser conforms to the protocol specification but does not claim to implement the JavaScript API. It can also be called a WebRTC device or native application.
  • A WebRTC endpoint is either of those two.
  • A WebRTC-compatible endpoint can communicate successfully with a WebRTC endpoint but may fail to meet some of its requirements. This specification does not constrain it.
sections.eli5: There are real players, partial players and guests. The rules are strictest for the web browsers, and guests can do their own thing.

sections.title: Pre- and Post-Processing
sections.content:
Unless the Session Description Protocol (SDP) or the codec says otherwise, the color space SHOULD be sRGB, and the video scan pattern is Y'CbCr 4:2:0.

For camera video the RFC sets no normative requirements. Implementors are encouraged to use automatic focus, white balance and light-level control where their platform allows, and to make the camera capture at the frame rate actually being encoded. For example, if encoding at 15 fps because of bandwidth or low light, the camera ideally captures at 15 fps rather than a higher rate.

For screen video (a desktop or an application window), the resolution can change midstream, for instance when a window is resized. Receivers MUST be prepared to handle midstream resolution changes in a way that preserves their utility. Exactly how, such as resizing the display element or scaling the stream, and whether to letterbox or pillarbox, is left to the application.

The default Y'CbCr 4:2:0 format is known to be less than optimal for screen content, which is generally RGB at 24 bits per sample or more. The RFC says that codecs optimized for screen content may become advisable in future.
sections.eli5: A camera should focus and adjust the light by itself. If someone shares their screen and resizes the window, the other side has to cope with the picture changing size.

sections.title: Stream Orientation
sections.content:
On mobile devices the camera orientation may not match the orientation the encoder uses, and it can change during a call, so the receiver must change how it renders the stream. The sender could rotate frames before encoding, but that may be impractical or inefficient, for example when the camera interface returns already compressed frames.

The RFC therefore relies on the Coordination of Video Orientation (CVO) mechanism from 3GPP TS 26.114. Implementations that can generate media in non-default orientations MUST support generating the R0 and R1 bits and MUST send them for all orientations when the peer indicates support. They MAY send the other CVO bits, including the higher-resolution rotation bits. All implementations SHOULD interpret R0 and R1 and MAY interpret the rest.

Some codecs have their own in-band orientation signal, such as the SEI Display Orientation messages in H.264 and H.265. If CVO has been negotiated, the sender MUST NOT use these. If CVO support is not signaled in the SDP, the sender MAY use them instead.
sections.eli5: If you turn your phone sideways during a call, the other person's screen has to know to turn the picture too. This RFC says how to pass along that turn.

sections.title: Mandatory-to-Implement Video Codecs
sections.content:
WebRTC browsers MUST implement the VP8 video codec as described in RFC 6386 and H.264 Constrained Baseline as described in ITU-T H.264. The same applies to WebRTC non-browsers that support transmitting or receiving video.

To promote non-royalty-bearing codecs, the RTCWEB working group and any successor groups intend to monitor the licensing landscape. If compelling evidence shows one of the two codecs is available royalty-free, the group plans to revisit which codecs are required for non-browsers. The royalty-free codec would stay mandatory and the other would become optional. This applies to non-browsers only, and there is no plan to revisit the codecs required for browsers.

WebRTC-compatible endpoints are free to implement any video codecs they see fit, though it is advisable to implement at least one of the codecs mandated for browsers.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to know two common picture languages, VP8 and H.264, so any two browsers always share at least one.

sections.title: Codec-Specific Requirements
sections.content:
For any codec, endpoints MAY send an a=imageattr attribute (from RFC 6236) to give the maximum resolution they want to receive, and senders SHOULD honor it. Unless SDP signals otherwise, receivers MUST be able to decode at least 20 fps at at least 320 by 240 pixels. Encoders are encouraged to support at least those values.

VP8: endpoints MUST support the payload formats in RFC 7741. VP8 encoders MUST limit their streams to the values receivers give in the max-fr and max-fs SDP attributes. Pixels are assumed square (1:1) unless signaled otherwise.

H.264: endpoints MUST support the payload formats in RFC 6184, MUST support Constrained Baseline Profile Level 1.2 and SHOULD support Constrained High Profile Level 1.3. To improve interoperability the RFC also fixes some optional parameters:

  • packetization-mode: mode 1 MUST be supported; other modes MAY be negotiated.
  • profile-level-id: MUST be included in SDP and MUST be interpreted on receipt.
  • max-mbps, max-smbps, max-fs, max-cpb, max-dpb, max-br: MAY be included, but SHOULD be interpreted when received so the sender can send the highest quality possible.
  • sprop-parameter-sets: this information MUST be signaled in-band, so implementations MUST NOT include this parameter in the SDP they generate.

H.264 codecs MAY send, and MUST correctly interpret, SEI filler payload and full frame freeze messages. Full frame freeze keeps the displayed picture stable while a video-switching MCU changes between input streams. Implementations MUST also be prepared to receive T.35 and unregistered user-data messages without ill effects, even if they ignore them.
sections.eli5: Both picture languages come with settings, like how big and how fast. This RFC says which settings every app must understand so they do not talk past each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new mechanisms or security concerns beyond those in the documents it references. In WebRTC, video is protected using DTLS and SRTP, and the full discussion is in the WebRTC security documents.

One specific warning is given. Variable bitrate codecs let an eavesdropper deduce the degree of inter-frame change, and by inference the amount of motion in the frame, from the stream's bitrate. Implementors should consider whether variable bitrate is appropriate for their application. Those using H.264 are also advised to read the security section of RFC 6184, with special regard to its normative requirement on SEI messages.
sections.eli5: Even a scrambled video can leak a little: a big burst of data means lots of movement. So pick your video settings with that in mind.
